result.summary: Achilles keeps dishonouring Hector's body until the gods intervene. Jove sends Thetis to Achilles and Iris to Priam, and Mercury guides Priam to Achilles' tent, where the two enemies weep together and Hector's body is ransomed. Hector is mourned and buried in Troy.

scenes.title: Achilles Drags Hector's Body
scenes.summary: Sleepless with grief for Patroclus, Achilles drags Hector's body round the tomb each dawn. Apollo shields it, and the gods want Mercury to steal it, though Juno, Neptune and Minerva object.
scenes.stakes: Hector's body is in danger of disfigurement, and Achilles risks the gods' anger.

scenes.title: Debate Among the Gods
scenes.summary: On the twelfth day Apollo rebukes the gods for neglecting Hector. Juno protests, but Jove decides Achilles must accept a ransom and asks for Thetis.
scenes.stakes: Divine unity, and the honour owed to Hector's remains.

scenes.title: Iris Fetches Thetis
scenes.summary: Iris dives to Thetis in her sea cave and brings her to Olympus. Jove tells her to make Achilles give up the body.
scenes.stakes: Thetis grieves for her doomed son and must carry Jove's command.

place.name: Sea between Samos and Imbrus, then Olympus

scenes.title: Thetis Persuades Achilles
scenes.summary: Thetis relays Jove's command, and Achilles agrees to accept a ransom.
scenes.stakes: Achilles risks Jove's anger if he refuses.

scenes.title: Priam Resolves to Go
scenes.summary: Iris tells the grieving Priam to ransom Hector. Hecuba begs him not to go, but he chooses the journey, gathers treasure and berates his sons.
scenes.stakes: Priam risks death at the hands of Achilles.

scenes.title: Prayer and Eagle Omen
scenes.summary: Priam prays to Jove, who sends an eagle. Priam sets out with Idaeus, and Jove sends Mercury to escort him.
scenes.stakes: Priam needs divine favour to survive the journey.

scenes.title: Mercury Guides Priam
scenes.summary: Mercury, disguised as a young Myrmidon, reassures Priam and drives him through the sleeping guards into Achilles' camp. He then reveals himself and departs.
scenes.stakes: Priam and Idaeus risk capture or death among the Achaeans.

place.name: Plain of Troy and the Achaean camp

scenes.title: Priam Supplicates Achilles
scenes.summary: Priam clasps Achilles' knees and appeals to him by his father. They weep together, Achilles agrees to the ransom and tells the tale of Niobe.
scenes.stakes: Priam risks death; Achilles risks sinning against Jove's word.

scenes.title: Supper, Truce, and Departure
scenes.summary: They eat, and Priam asks for a truce of eleven days. Mercury wakes Priam, who leaves secretly with Hector's body.
scenes.stakes: Priam could be discovered and held captive by the Achaeans.

place.name: Achilles' tent and the ford of Xanthus

scenes.title: Lament and Funeral of Hector
scenes.summary: Cassandra sees the returning wagon, and Andromache, Hecuba and Helen lament. Hector is burned and buried after nine days of gathering wood.
scenes.stakes: Troy's fate after losing its defender.

characters.name: Alexandrus
characters.description: Trojan prince who judged the goddesses, Helen's husband

characters.name: Niobe
characters.description: Mother whose children were slain, turned to stone

alias_notes.explanation: Another name for Paris, who judged the goddesses.

notable_quotes.reason: Achilles' image of Jove's two urns of good and evil gifts.
Priam's plea: he has kissed the hand of his son's killer.
Closing line of the poem, marking Hector's funeral.

analysis.text: The book resolves Achilles' wrath through shared grief and pity. Enemies recognise common mortality, as Priam calls up Achilles' father.
The episode reflects Greek values of supplication, hospitality and proper burial. Even enemies owed the dead funeral rites.

legacy.text: The meeting of Priam and Achilles became a model for scenes of compassion toward an enemy in later literature and art.
Troy (2004) adapts the scene of Priam visiting Achilles to ransom Hector.

fun_facts.text: The ending of the Iliad is Hector's funeral; it does not narrate the fall of Troy.

language_notes.text: "Bethought them of" means turned their thoughts to; the people remembered sleep as a welcome gift after supper.
"Slayer of Argus" is a standard title of Mercury, who killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus.
Refers to the Judgement of Paris (Alexandrus): he judged Venus fairest over Juno and Minerva, accepting Helen as her bribe, which caused the Trojan War.
"Burn you thigh-bones" is an old construction meaning burn for you; thigh bones wrapped in fat were the gods' share of sacrifice.
"Ruth" means pity or compassion, so "neither right nor ruth" means no sense of justice or mercy.
"Banes" and "boons" are used as verbs: conscience harms or benefits a man, depending on whether he heeds it.
"Let him bide" means let him rest, accepting the loss and leaving the dead in peace.
Juno claims to have raised Thetis, the sea goddess, who is Achilles' mother.
The wedding of Peleus and Thetis was attended by the gods; Apollo played the lyre there. Juno sneers at him as untrustworthy.
"Fleet as the wind" is a stock comparison; Iris is the divine messenger, here swift as the wind that carries her.
The sinking lead is the weight on a fishing line, which was threaded through a piece of ox-horn so the line would not be bitten through by fish.
Thetis already knows Achilles is fated to die at Troy, far from his home in Phthia; hence her mourning before his death.
"Sombre" means dark and gloomy; the black veil signals mourning.
"This nine days past" means for the last nine days; the gods' quarrel has lasted that long.
Mercury is called slayer of Argus for killing the hundred-eyed giant Argus, who guarded Io. It hints he is a skilled thief and fit for stealing the body.
"These too were well" means eating and love are also good and fitting; Thetis urges him to return to normal life despite grief.
Ilius is another name for Troy (Ilium), the city whose king is Priam.
"Slayer of Argus" is Mercury (Hermes), who killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus; here he is to act as Priam's guide.
"Take heed to his ways and sin not" means Achilles will watch his conduct and avoid wrongdoing toward a suppliant.
"Filth" and "mire" refer to dung and mud Priam smeared on himself in mourning; "grovelling" means lying face down.
Dardanus was the ancestor of the Trojan royal line, so "offspring of Dardanus" is a formal address to Priam.
Hecuba refers to the Fates spinning a person's destiny like thread at birth; she wishes to eat Achilles' liver in revenge.
"A bird of ill omen" means a bringer of bad luck; Hecuba's warnings are likened to an ominous bird's cry.
Priam says he would distrust a human prophet or priest, but a goddess seen face to face (Iris) is certain.
A talent was a measure of weight, here of gold; a tripod was a three-legged cauldron stand, valued as a gift.
The house of Hades is the underworld; Priam prefers death to seeing Troy sacked.
"Heroes of the dance" is scornful: Priam calls his surviving sons dancers and thieves rather than warriors.
A cubit was roughly the length of a forearm, about half a metre; the yoke-band was a leather binding.
A drink-offering (libation) was wine poured out to a god while praying.
The bird of omen is the eagle, sacred to Jove; its appearance on the right was a favourable sign.
"Upon my right hand": birds seen on the right were favorable omens, so Priam asks for the sign to appear on that side.
"Portent" means an omen, a sign from the gods about what will happen.
"Waggon" is an older spelling of wagon; here it is the four-wheeled cart carrying the ransom for Hector's body.
Ilius is another name for Troy, here meaning the city itself.
"Ken" means range of sight or knowledge; to escape the ken of Jove is to escape his notice.
"Slayer of Argus" refers to Mercury killing the hundred-eyed watchman Argus, a traditional epithet of the god.
"Hey-day" means the peak or fullest bloom of youth.
Ilius is the founder-king of Troy, after whom Ilium (Ilius) is named; his tomb was a landmark on the plain.
"Descendant of Dardanus" addresses Priam by his ancestor, the legendary founder of the Trojan royal line.
"The bringer of good luck" is an epithet for Mercury, who is still disguised and unnamed here.
"Slayer of Argus" refers to Mercury killing the hundred-eyed giant Argus, set by Juno to watch Io.
"You would prove me" means you are testing me.
Achilles withdrew from fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon, the son of Atreus, over the captive Briseis.
The sepulchre is the tomb of Patroclus, whose death Achilles avenges by dragging Hector's body.
A chalice is a drinking cup, here a valuable gift offered as a bribe.
Tussock-grass is coarse grass growing in clumps, used here as thatch.
"Of the race of Mars" means Alcimus was a warrior of Mars's stock, i.e. martial; Mars is the Roman name for the war god (Greek Ares).
The simile describes a fugitive murderer seeking refuge abroad; onlookers are astonished at his arrival, as Achilles is at Priam's.
"Steeled myself" means hardened himself to do what no one has done: kiss the hand of his son's killer.
"Unburthened" is an archaic spelling of unburdened; "sated" means fully satisfied.
The two urns of Jove, one of good gifts and one of evil, are Achilles' explanation of why mortals suffer.
Lesbos, Phrygia and the Hellespont mark the limits of Priam's former wealthy realm in the north-east Aegean region.
Achilles' mother is the sea goddess Thetis, daughter of the old man of the sea; Jove sent her with his command.
"Waggon" is the older spelling of wagon; here it is the cart carrying the ransom.
Niobe was a mother whose children were killed after she boasted of them; Achilles uses her as an example of grief that still yields to hunger.
"Ilius" is another name for Ilium, i.e. Troy.
Dardanus was the legendary ancestor of the Trojan royal line, so "descendant of Dardanus" simply means Priam the Trojan king.
"Grovelled" means lay prostrate in grief; "mire" is mud, here the filth of the stable-yard where Priam rolled in mourning.
"Lie outside" means in the open forecourt, away from the hut, so that visiting counsellors would not find Priam inside.
"Pent up" means shut in. The Trojans fear leaving the walls, so fetching wood from the distant mountain is dangerous.
Taking the wrist was a gesture of pledge and reassurance, confirming the truce and that Priam need not fear.
Xanthus is the river of Troy, here called a child of Jove (the Greek Zeus), as rivers were thought divine.
Pergamus is the citadel of Troy, the high fortified part of the city.
Dirge: a song of mourning. Minstrels were hired to lead the lament and the women answered.
"Bitten the dust" means fallen dead in battle, here said of the Achaeans (Greeks) Hector killed.
Apollo's "painless shafts" refers to the belief that gentle sudden deaths of men were Apollo's arrows; Hecuba says Hector looks peacefully slain.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, who carried Helen off to Troy, causing the war.
Argives is another name for the Greeks, here the besieging army.
They quenched the pyre with wine, then gathered the bones, a standard cremation rite.

context_notes.text: The aegis is a divine shield or breastplate, here used by Apollo, who protects Hector's body from harm.
Juno, Neptune and Minerva (Jove's grey-eyed daughter) sided with the Greeks and hated Troy.
Thetis is a sea goddess and Achilles' mother; Jove will use her to persuade her son to give up the body.
Saturn is the father of Jove; the Greek equivalent is Cronus. "All-seeing" marks Jove as the god who surveys everything.
Offering a cup was a gesture of hospitality and welcome among Homeric hosts, here showing Juno's sympathy for Thetis.
Ransoming a slain warrior's body with gifts was a recognised custom, and Jove is setting up Priam's journey to Achilles.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) is angry because Achilles keeps dishonouring Hector's corpse, dragging it and refusing burial.
The son of Saturn is Jove, whose father was the Titan Saturn (the Greek Cronus). Iris is the gods' winged messenger.
A cedar-wood store-room shows Priam's wealth; he will draw from these treasures to pay Hector's ransom.
Priam brings costly goods as ransom. The Thracians were northern neighbours; such gifts marked guest-friendship and diplomacy.
Priam's sons include Helenus, a seer, Paris, who caused the war, and Deiphobus, a leading warrior.
Washing the hands with pure water was a ritual purification before praying to Jove.
Washing the hands and pouring a drink-offering (libation) of wine was the usual ritual before praying to a god.
Mercury was the god who guided travelers and escorted souls, which is why Jove chooses him to lead Priam safely to Achilles.
Mercury's golden sandals and sleep-inducing wand are his standard equipment, used here to hide Priam from the Greeks.
The Myrmidons are Achilles' followers from Phthia; Mercury's invented family details make the disguise convincing.
Twelve days is how long Achilles has mistreated Hector's body; the gods, especially Apollo, have preserved it.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) is messenger and guide of travellers; his father is Jove (Zeus).
Kissing a man's hands and clasping his knees was the formal gesture of a suppliant begging for mercy or protection.
Peleus, Achilles' father, was king of the Myrmidons and married the sea goddess Thetis.
Achilles speaks to the dead Patroclus, whose death he is avenging, since he fears Patroclus will resent Hector's return.
Leto was mother of Apollo and Diana (the Greek Artemis), who punished Niobe's boast by killing her children.
Automedon was Achilles' charioteer and trusted companion, who here serves the meal.
Briseis was the captive woman taken from Achilles by Agamemnon, whose seizure began his quarrel; she was later returned to him.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) is messenger of the gods and guide of travellers, which is why he helps Priam.
Cassandra is Priam's daughter, a prophetess doomed never to be believed.
Andromache is Hector's wife; her son Astyanax is the child she fears for.
Achilles had dragged Hector's body around the tomb of his friend Patroclus, whom Hector had killed.
Nine days of gathering wood matches the truce Achilles granted Priam for the burial.

literary_notes.text: Sleep is treated as a mighty power before whom all bow, yet he cannot touch Achilles, stressing the depth of his grief.
Achilles is compared to a ravening lion, portraying him as a pitiless beast acting without restraint.
Apollo sets ordinary grief, which fades, against Achilles' endless rage, making his behavior seem excessive.
Juno's bitter insult to Apollo shows her partisan, quarrelsome nature and her lasting pride in her role with Achilles.
Iris's plunge into the sea is likened to a lead weight dropping through the water, giving a sense of speed and depth.
Thetis weeping for her son's coming death in advance reminds us of Achilles' doom, which hangs over the whole poem.
The waves "opened a path" for the goddesses, as if the sea obeyed and honoured them.
"Silver-footed" is Thetis's recurring epithet, which gives her a formal, divine dignity even as she descends in grief.
Thetis's remark that Achilles has little time to live recalls his fated early death, which hangs over the poem.
Iris is compared to the wind, conveying the speed of the divine messenger.
Tear-wet clothes and a filth-covered old king vividly show the household's grief and Priam's humiliation.
"Iron courage" suggests a hardness needed to face Achilles; Hecuba also calls him a savage, showing her fear and hatred.
Priam's readiness to die if he may first hold his son stirs sympathy and shows his devotion.
Priam's harsh outburst shows a grieving father lashing out, in contrast with his later humility before Achilles.
Priam turns his grief into anger, accusing the Trojans of adding to his sorrow.
Hector is praised as a god among men, so great that he seemed an immortal's son.
The eagle's wingspan is compared to a rich man's well-bolted door, giving a homely measure of its enormous size.
The eagle's favorable omen on the right and the Trojans' renewed comfort hint that the dangerous mission will succeed.
The mourners wail as though Priam were going to his death, hinting at the real danger of his journey.
Mercury's disguise as a handsome young man shows his gentle, helpful nature toward Priam.
The hair standing on end vividly conveys Priam's terror.
The disguised god says Priam reminds him of his father, while the reader knows Mercury's real father is Jove.
Hector's body is better preserved in death than a living man's, a hint of divine care for him.
Hector lies "fresh as dew," suggesting purity and miraculous preservation.
Mercury's sleep over the guards shows the gods steering the plot to enable Priam's journey.
Priam asks Achilles to picture his own father, turning Achilles' love for Peleus into the bridge for compassion.
Two enemies weep side by side, each for a different loss, showing shared human grief overcoming hatred.
"The hand of famine" personifies hunger as a pursuer, vividly picturing the fate of the man given only evil gifts.
Comparing Achilles to a lion springing recalls his fierce nature even as he acts with kindness.
Niobe's story is a mythic parallel to Priam's loss, used to persuade him that even great grief allows eating.
Each man marvels at the other, a mirrored admiration that shows the enemies recognising shared humanity.
Mercury mocks Priam's calm sleep among enemies, stressing the danger Priam has overlooked.
"Dawn in robe of saffron" is a formulaic Homeric epithet, personifying daybreak as a goddess in a saffron-coloured gown.
Cassandra is compared to golden Venus (Aphrodite), stressing her beauty at the moment she brings the grief into the open.
Andromache predicts the fall of Troy, which Hector's death makes certain, though the poem ends before it.
Hector, though mutilated, lies fresh as dew, a tender image of the gods' protection of his body.
The formulaic "rosy-fingered dawn" marks the passing of time and gives the ending a calm, ritual tone.
Ending on "tamer of horses" gives Hector a final honorific, closing the epic with his memory.
